deposit_max: One month's periodic rent, except for pets, changes to the premises, or increased liability risks to the landlord or premises, for which more may be taken (35-9A-201(a)). No interest or separate-account requirement found in 35-9A-201.
deposit_interest: No interest or escrow requirement found in 35-9A-201.
late_fee_rule: No statutory cap, grace period or limit on residential late fees found in the Alabama URLTA (35-9A); the only reference is 35-9A-421(b), which lets a nonpayment termination notice list 'late fees owed'. A late fee must come from the lease. Other Code titles were not searched.
late_fee_citation: Ala. Code 35-9A-421(b) (no late-fee limit found in 35-9A)
entry_notice: Landlord may enter at reasonable times after giving at least two days' notice of intent to enter (posting a note on the primary door stating the time and purpose is a permitted method), unless impracticable. No notice needed for emergencies, court order, or if tenant has been given a separate general notice/advance schedule of more than two days for repairs or services; entry also allowed with reasonable cause to believe the unit is abandoned or during tenant absence over 14 days (35-9A-303, 35-9A-423(b)).
month_to_month_tenant_notice: At least 30 days' written notice before the periodic rental date specified in the notice (35-9A-441(b)).
month_to_month_landlord_notice: Same: at least 30 days' written notice before the periodic rental date specified in the notice (35-9A-441(b)). For nonpayment the landlord may give a written notice with at least seven business days to pay (35-9A-421(b)).
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No statewide rent control law found; counties and municipalities may not enact or enforce ordinances controlling the amount of rent charged for leasing private property (Ala. Code 11-80-8.1(b)). No statute in 35-9A requiring advance notice of a rent increase was found.
rent_increase_citation: Ala. Code 11-80-8.1; 35-9A-121 (no rent-increase notice provision found in 35-9A)
retaliation_rule: A landlord may not retaliate by discriminatorily increasing rent, decreasing services, or bringing or threatening an action for possession because the tenant complained to a code-enforcement agency, complained to the landlord of a 35-9A-204 violation, or joined a tenant organization. Tenant gets the 35-9A-407 remedies (up to 3 months' rent or actual damages, plus attorney's fees) and a defense to possession. Exceptions: tenant-caused code violation, rent default, code compliance requiring alteration/demolition, other material lease violations (35-9A-501(c)). No time-based presumption.

deposit_max: Two months' periodic rent for prepaid rent and security deposit combined; the cap does not apply to units where the rent exceeds $2,000 a month. A landlord may take an additional pet deposit of up to one month's rent for a tenant with a pet that is not a service animal; it must be accounted for separately and used only for pet-related damage (§ 34.03.070(a), (h)).
deposit_interest: No interest requirement in § 34.03.070. The landlord must promptly deposit the money, where practicable, in a trust account, and may not commingle it with other funds (§ 34.03.070(c)).
late_fee_rule: No provision on residential late fees found in AS 34.03 (the Act's sections were read in full). Any late fee must come from the lease. A rental agreement cannot waive the tenant's rights under the Act (§ 34.03.040(a)(1)). Other chapters of the code were not searched.
entry_notice: The landlord must give the tenant at least 24 hours' notice of intent to enter, except in an emergency or if it is impracticable, and may enter only at reasonable times and with the tenant's consent; the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent (to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs, supply services, or show the unit to buyers, mortgagees, tenants, workers or contractors). The landlord may enter without consent in an emergency, and may not abuse access or use it to harass. If the landlord makes an unlawful entry or repeated harassing demands, the tenant can get an injunction or terminate on 10 days' written notice and recover the greater of actual damages or one month's rent, plus court costs and attorney fees (§ 34.03.300(b)).
month_to_month_tenant_notice: Written notice to the landlord at least 30 days before the rental due date specified in the notice (§ 34.03.290(b)). For a week-to-week tenancy: written notice at least 14 days before the termination date, while rent is current (§ 34.03.290(a)).
month_to_month_landlord_notice: Same as the tenant: written notice at least 30 days before the rental due date specified in the notice for a month-to-month tenancy (14 days for week-to-week). Separately, for nonpayment the landlord may terminate if rent is not paid within 7 days after written notice (§ 34.03.220(b)); for a material lease breach or a health and safety violation the notice to quit is at least 10 days, and 24 hours to 5 days for deliberate substantial damage or illegal activity (§ 34.03.220(a)).
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No rent control or rent-increase notice provision found in AS 34.03. A landlord may not retaliate by increasing rent after a protected tenant action (§ 34.03.310(a)), subject to the exceptions in § 34.03.310(d).
retaliation_rule: A landlord may not retaliate by increasing rent, decreasing services, or bringing or threatening an action for possession after the tenant complained to the landlord of a habitability violation (§ 34.03.100), sought to enforce rights under the Act, joined a tenants' union, or complained to a governmental agency about housing, wage, price or rent controls. The tenant has the remedies in § 34.03.210 (recover possession or terminate, plus up to 1.5 times actual damages) and a defense to an eviction action. Exceptions: the landlord may still seek possession for unpaid rent, code-required work, waste or nuisance or illegal use, or in good faith for personal use, remodeling or demolition, or conversion out of residential use, and may raise rent for substantial tax or operating-cost increases, a capital improvement, or to match market rent (§ 34.03.310(c), (d)).

deposit_max: 1.5 months' rent (all security, however named, including prepaid rent; a tenant may voluntarily prepay more rent). The purpose of any nonrefundable fee must be stated in writing; any fee not designated nonrefundable is refundable.
late_fee_rule: No statutory cap found; the statute refers to a 'reasonable late fee set forth in a written rental agreement'.
entry_notice: At least two days' notice and entry only at reasonable times, except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable. Landlord may not abuse access or use it to harass the tenant.
month_to_month_tenant_notice: 30 days (written, before the periodic rental date)
month_to_month_landlord_notice: 30 days (written, before the periodic rental date)
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No; cities and towns may not control rents on private residential property (state preemption).
retaliation_rule: Landlord may not retaliate (raise rent, cut services, or bring/threaten eviction) because a tenant complained to a housing-code agency, complained to the landlord about repairs, or joined a tenants' union. A complaint within 6 months before the act creates a presumption of retaliation.

deposit_max: Two months' periodic rent, however denominated (18-16-304). The deposit rules do not apply to dwelling units owned by an individual who (with spouse, minor children and related rental entities) owns five or fewer dwelling units, unless a third party manages them for a fee, including rent collection (18-16-303).
deposit_interest: No interest or separate-account requirement found in 18-16-301 to 18-16-306.
late_fee_rule: No late-fee provision found in the Arkansas landlord-tenant sections read (18-16-301 to -306 and the 18-17 sections listed in the notes). Any late fee must come from the lease; no statutory cap or fee grace period found. Other titles of the Arkansas Code were not searched.
late_fee_citation: Ark. Code 18-16-301 to 18-16-306, 18-17 (no late-fee provision found; 18-17-401(a) lets the lease set terms, 18-60-304(3) 3-day notice to quit)
entry_notice: No fixed advance-notice period for entry is stated. A tenant 'shall not unreasonably withhold consent' to the landlord entering to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs, supply services, investigate lease violations or possible criminal activity, or show the unit to purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers or contractors (18-17-602(a)). If the tenant refuses lawful access, the landlord can seek an injunction in district court to compel access or terminate the rental agreement, plus actual damages and attorney's fees (18-17-705).
month_to_month_tenant_notice: At least 30 days' written notice before the termination date specified in the notice (18-17-704(b)). Week-to-week tenancies: 7 days (18-17-704(a)).
month_to_month_landlord_notice: Same: at least 30 days' written notice before the termination date (18-17-704(b)). For unpaid rent, the landlord may terminate if rent is not paid within 5 days of the due date (18-17-701(b)); for other lease violations, written notice ending the lease not less than 14 days after receipt if not remedied (18-17-701(a)).
rent_increase_notice: No statute requiring advance notice of a rent increase found in 18-16 or 18-17.
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No rent control: Arkansas preempts local rent, rental application fee and rental deposit control (Ark. Code 14-16-601 and 14-54-1409, as amended by Act 459 of 2025), except that the state's two-month deposit cap (18-16-304) still applies.

deposit_max: 1 month's rent for most landlords (since July 1, 2024, AB 12); 2 months for small landlords (a natural person, or an LLC whose members are all natural persons, owning at most 2 residential rental properties with at most 4 units total). The small-landlord exception does not apply to service-member tenants. Deposits can never be 'non-refundable'.
late_fee_rule: No fixed cap. Under Civ. Code 1671(d), a liquidated-damages clause (such as a late fee) in a residential lease is void unless it would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix the actual damage, so the fee should be a genuine estimate of the landlord's cost of late payment. Large flat or daily fees are most exposed to a penalty challenge.
entry_notice: 24 hours' written notice is presumed reasonable (6 days if mailed); entry only for listed purposes and normally during business hours; emergencies excepted.
month_to_month_tenant_notice: 30 days
month_to_month_landlord_notice: 30 days if tenancy under 1 year; 60 days if 1 year or more. After 12 months most tenancies also need 'just cause' (Tenant Protection Act).
rent_increase_notice: 30 days' notice for increases of 10% or less; 90 days for more than 10% (month-to-month).
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: Yes for many units: Tenant Protection Act caps yearly increases at 5% + local CPI, max 10% (exemptions incl. buildings under 15 years old and many single-family homes with proper notice).
retaliation_rule: Landlord may not retaliate (rent increase, reduced services, eviction) within 180 days after the tenant exercises legal rights such as complaining about habitability.

deposit_max: 2 months' rent (since Aug 7, 2023).
late_fee_rule: Only if disclosed in the lease, rent is at least 7 calendar days late, and the landlord gives written notice of the fee within 180 days of the due date; capped at the greater of $50 or 5% of the past-due rent (several fees for one late payment only if the total stays within that cap); no interest on late fees; no eviction or termination for unpaid late fees; no late fee on the part of rent a subsidy provider pays. Non-complying lease terms are void.
month_to_month_tenant_notice: Written notice by tenancy period: 21 days for a month-to-month tenancy (1 month to <6 months); 28 days (6 months to <1 year); 91 days (1 year or longer); 3 days for week-to-week.
month_to_month_landlord_notice: Same notice periods, but since Apr 19, 2024 (HB24-1098) a landlord generally needs cause to evict, with certain exceptions; listed no-fault grounds include demolition or conversion, substantial renovation, landlord or family moving in, selling the home, the tenant refusing a new lease with reasonable terms, and a history of nonpayment.
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No; counties and municipalities are prohibited from enacting rent control (C.R.S. 38-12-301).
retaliation_rule: Landlord may not raise rent, cut services, end the lease, threaten eviction or otherwise intimidate a tenant for a good-faith habitability or health/safety complaint, or for joining or organizing a tenants' association; the tenant may end the lease and recover the greater of 3 months' rent or 3x actual damages, plus attorney fees, and can raise retaliation as a defense to eviction.

deposit_max: Two months' rent for a tenant under 62; one month's rent for a tenant 62 or older (a landlord who took more than one month's rent from a tenant who later turns 62 must return the excess on request). Advance payment of the first month's rent and a key or special-equipment deposit are not 'security deposit'. The landlord must immediately put the deposit in an escrow account at a Connecticut financial institution and, within 30 days of receiving it, tell the tenant in writing the amount and the name and address of the institution. A landlord may not charge a move-in or move-out fee (47a-4d(b)).
deposit_interest: Yes. The landlord must pay interest each year at a rate not less than the 'deposit index' set under section 36a-26 (never waivable by lease, 47a-4(a)(4)). Interest is paid to the tenant or credited toward rent on the tenancy anniversary, and if the tenancy ends or the deposit is returned earlier, within 21 days after that. No interest is owed for any month in which the tenant was more than 10 days late with rent, unless the landlord imposed a late charge.
late_fee_rule: A late charge is allowed only if the written rental agreement provides for it, and only after the grace period: 9 days after the due date (4 days for a one-week tenancy). Since January 1, 2026, the grace period is 5 days longer if the landlord's online rent payment system prevents the tenant from paying on time. The charge may not exceed the lesser of $5 per day up to $50, or 5% of the delinquent rent (5% of the tenant's share if a government or charity pays part of the rent), and only one late charge may be assessed per late payment. A lease clause that charges earlier or more is unenforceable.
entry_notice: No fixed number of hours or days in the statute. The landlord must give reasonable written or oral notice of the intent to enter and may enter only at reasonable times, except in an emergency. The tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to entry to inspect, make agreed repairs or improvements, supply agreed services or show the unit to buyers, mortgagees, tenants, workers or contractors. Without consent the landlord may enter only in an emergency, during a tenant's extended absence (if the tenant was to notify the landlord), under a court order, or if the tenant abandoned or surrendered the unit. If the landlord enters unlawfully or makes repeated demands that unreasonably harass, the tenant may recover actual damages of at least one month's rent plus reasonable attorney's fees, and may seek an injunction or end the lease.
month_to_month_tenant_notice: Connecticut statute sets no notice period for a tenant ending a month-to-month tenancy. Unless the lease fixes a term, the tenancy runs month to month (week to week if rent is weekly) (47a-3b). Check the lease terms.
month_to_month_landlord_notice: Written notice to quit possession, delivered at least 3 days before the lease ends or the date stated in the notice, on a ground in 47a-23(a): lapse of time, lease violation, nonpayment of rent after the grace period, nuisance and others. The notice must use the statutory form and state the reason. For nonpayment, the notice may be delivered in the month after the unpaid month and still ends the tenancy. A landlord must then bring a court summary process action; self-help eviction is not allowed. Tenants aged 62+ or with a disability in buildings of 5+ units may be evicted only for the good causes in 47a-23c(b).
rent_increase_notice: No rent increase is effective unless the landlord gave the tenant written notice at least 45 days before the date the increase takes effect (for a lease term of one month or less, notice equal to a full term of the lease). The tenant's silence is not agreement. Rent cannot be raised during the term of a rental agreement. Applies to rental agreements entered into, renewed or extended on or after October 1, 2024. For tenants aged 62+ or disabled in buildings of 5+ units, increases must be 'fair and equitable' under 7-148c and can be challenged at the fair rent commission or in court (47a-23c(c)). An increase demanded within six months after a protected tenant complaint is retaliation unless an exception applies (47a-20, 47a-20a).
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No statewide rent control found in chapters 830-832; the statute only requires notice and bars increases mid-term.
retaliation_rule: A landlord may not bring a possession action, demand a rent increase or decrease services within six months after the tenant in good faith tried to fix a code violation by any lawful means (including complaining to officials or a fair rent commission), a municipal agency filed a notice, complaint or order, the tenant asked for repairs, started an action under 47a-14h, or organized or joined a tenants' union. Exceptions: nonpayment or lease violation, landlord needs the unit for own home in good faith, condition caused by the tenant or their guest, a notice to end a periodic tenancy given before the complaint; and a rent increase is allowed if the tenant caused the condition or the landlord's taxes or operating costs substantially rose (47a-20a).

deposit_max: 1 month's rent when the lease is for 1 year or more, and for month-to-month tenancies once they have lasted 1 year (any excess must then be credited back). These limits do not apply to furnished units. A separate pet deposit is capped at 1 month's rent, and none may be charged for a certified, trained support animal of a disabled resident. The deposit must sit in a designated escrow account at a federally insured bank with an office in Delaware, and the landlord must tell the tenant where it is.
deposit_interest: No interest requirement in § 5514.
late_fee_rule: Where the lease provides for a late charge, it is capped at 5% of the monthly rent and counts as additional rent, and no late charge may be imposed until rent is more than 5 days late. If the landlord keeps no office or permanent place in the county where rent can be paid, the due date is extended by 3 days.
entry_notice: At least 48 hours' notice, entry only between 8:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m.; no notice needed for repairs the tenant requested or in an emergency. The tenant may waive the 48-hour notice only for showings to prospective tenants or buyers, in a separate signed addendum or document. Access may not be abused or used to harass.
month_to_month_tenant_notice: 60 days' written notice, counted from the first day of the month after notice is given
month_to_month_landlord_notice: 60 days' written notice, counted from the first day of the month after notice is given (also 60 days before the end of a fixed term)
rent_increase_notice: To renew with a higher rent or other changed terms, the landlord must give at least 60 days' written notice before the lease expires, stating the changes and their effective date. The tenant has until 45 days before the end of the term to reject them; rejecting acts as a termination notice.
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: The Residential Landlord-Tenant Code sets no limit on the amount of rent; it regulates the notice for increases.
retaliation_rule: A landlord may not seek possession, raise rent or cut services because the tenant made a good-faith code complaint, a government authority filed a violation notice, the tenant organized or is an officer of a tenant organization, or the tenant pursued a legal right. Such action within 90 days of the complaint or act is presumed retaliatory.

deposit_max: One full month's rent (the first full month's rent charged), and it may be charged only once. Must be held in an interest-bearing escrow account at a D.C. financial institution, and the lease or receipt must state the terms of the deposit.
deposit_interest: Yes: at no less than the statement savings rate of the bank holding the escrow account (reset each Jan 1 and Jul 1), payable at the end of tenancies of 12 months or more.
deposit_citation: 14 DCMR §§ 308.2-308.3, 309.1-309.2, 311.1-311.2; D.C. Code § 42-3502.17(c), (e) (D.C. Law 26-156, eff. Aug. 14, 2026: written notice of alleged unpaid amounts within 45 days, 30-day tenant dispute, 10-day landlord response)
late_fee_rule: Capped at 5% of the full amount of rent due, and only if the written lease states the maximum late fee. It can be charged only if rent is still unpaid 5 days after the due date (or a longer grace period in the lease), only once per late payment, with no interest on it, and never for rent a subsidy provider is responsible for. A landlord may not evict for an unpaid late fee or deduct it from a later rent payment; unpaid lawfully imposed late fees may be deducted from the security deposit at the end of the tenancy.
entry_notice: At least 48 hours' written notice (email or text allowed), only for a reasonable purpose such as repairs, inspection or showing the unit, and only between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m., not on Sundays or federal holidays, unless the tenant agrees otherwise. No notice needed in an emergency.
month_to_month_tenant_notice: 30 days' written notice, expiring on the first day of the first month at least 30 days after the notice. A lease may not require more than 30 days' notice to vacate unless it also requires the landlord to give at least that much notice of any rent increase.
month_to_month_landlord_notice: No notice-only termination: a tenant who keeps paying rent cannot be evicted even after the lease expires, except for a cause listed in § 42-3505.01 and after the written notice that section requires.
rent_increase_notice: For units under D.C. rent stabilization, no increase takes effect until the first rent day more than 60 calendar days after written notice.
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: Yes, rent stabilization covers many D.C. rental units (exemptions in § 42-3502.05): increases for occupied units are limited to the annual adjustment of general applicability (CPI-W) plus 2%, never more than 10%, and only once every 12 months.
retaliation_rule: Landlord may not retaliate (eviction, rent increase, cut in services, refusal to renew, harassment) against a tenant who exercises legal rights. Retaliation is presumed if, within the prior 6 months, the tenant asked for code repairs, complained to D.C. officials, joined a tenant organization, or sued the landlord; the landlord must rebut by clear and convincing evidence.

deposit_max: No statutory cap.
deposit_interest: Landlord must tell the tenant in writing within 30 days how and where the deposit is held; if it is held in an interest-bearing account, the tenant is owed at least 75% of the account's annualized average rate or 5% per year simple interest, whichever the landlord elects. Deductions require written notice of claim, sent by certified mail within 30 days after the lease ends.
late_fee_rule: No statutory cap and no late-fee section in the Florida Residential Landlord and Tenant Act; a late fee exists only if the written lease provides it (rent may include other payments the lease designates as rent).
entry_notice: 24 hours' notice for repairs, entry between 7:30 a.m. and 8:00 p.m.; emergencies excepted.
month_to_month_tenant_notice: 30 days' written notice before the end of a monthly period
month_to_month_landlord_notice: 30 days' written notice before the end of a monthly period
rent_increase_notice: No separate statute; for month-to-month tenancies a change effectively needs the 30-day termination notice (83.57).
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No. Local rent control is barred except under a narrow housing-emergency procedure (125.0103), and local regulation of residential tenancies is preempted to the state (83.425).
retaliation_rule: Landlord may not retaliate against good-faith complaints or tenant organizing.

deposit_max: 2 months' rent (leases entered/renewed on or after July 1, 2024).
late_fee_rule: No Georgia statute found that caps residential late fees or sets a rent grace period; any late fee comes from the lease. O.C.G.A. 44-7-50(c) (2024 amendment, leases entered into or renewed on or after 7/1/2024) requires a written notice to vacate or pay all past due rent, late fees, utilities and other charges within three business days before the landlord can file for eviction. O.C.G.A. 44-7-34 lets the landlord keep the security deposit for nonpayment of rent or fees for late payment. Sections searched: 44-7-1 to 44-7-54 (selected) and 13-6-7; whether a very high fee is an unenforceable penalty was not verified.
entry_notice: No statute; follow the lease.
month_to_month_tenant_notice: 30 days
month_to_month_landlord_notice: 60 days
rent_increase_notice: Month-to-month (tenancy at will): the landlord must give 60 days' notice to change the rent, the same notice needed to end the tenancy.
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No; local rent control is preempted (O.C.G.A. 44-7-19).
retaliation_rule: Retaliation for good-faith repair requests or complaints to authorities is prohibited.

deposit_max: One month's rent, plus (if the landlord and tenant agree) an additional pet-damage deposit of up to one more month's rent; the pet amount may not be required from a tenant without a pet or for an assistance animal that is a reasonable accommodation (HRS 521-44(b)). The deposit may be held only for: tenant defaults (damage from failure to comply with 521-51, unpaid rent, unreturned keys/fobs/openers/mailbox keys), cleaning to the condition at move-in, damages if the tenant wrongfully quits, pet damage, and unpaid landlord-supplied utilities (521-44(a)). At the start of the tenancy the landlord may not require or receive any money other than the first month's rent and the security deposit (521-44(b)). The deposit is not last month's rent unless agreed in writing and the tenant gives 45 days' notice (521-44(b)). The tenant's claim to the deposit is prior to any creditor of the landlord, even if commingled (521-44(b)).
deposit_interest: No interest or separate-account requirement found in HRS 521-44 (deposits may be commingled).
late_fee_rule: If the rental agreement provides for a late charge for rent not paid when due, the late charge may not exceed 8 percent of the amount of rent due (HRS 521-21(f)). The statute does not require a grace period or prior written notice of the fee.
entry_notice: Except in an emergency or where impracticable, the landlord must give the tenant at least two days' notice of intent to enter and may enter only during reasonable hours; the landlord may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant (HRS 521-53(b)). The tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to entry to inspect, make necessary or agreed repairs or alterations, supply agreed services, or show the unit to prospective purchasers, mortgagees or tenants (521-53(a)). No other right of entry exists except by court order, if the tenant appears to have abandoned the premises, or as permitted by 521-70(b) (521-53(c)). A tenant may treat repeated demands for unreasonable entry, or unreasonable unconsented entry, as grounds to terminate the rental agreement and a circuit judge may enjoin the landlord and fine up to $100 (521-73(c)). The landlord is liable for theft, casualty or other damage from an entry without the tenant's actual consent (except in an emergency such as fire) and any agreement exempting the landlord from this liability is void (521-73(b), (d)).
month_to_month_tenant_notice: Written notice at least 28 days before the anticipated termination; the tenant owes rent through the 28th day (HRS 521-71(b)).
month_to_month_landlord_notice: Written notice at least 45 days before the anticipated termination; the tenant may vacate any time in the last 45 days but must notify the landlord of the vacate date and pay prorated rent (521-71(a)). If the landlord plans voluntary demolition, condominium conversion or a change to transient vacation rentals, written notice at least 120 days (521-71(c)). For tenancies shorter than month-to-month, either side gives at least 10 days' notice (521-71(d)). For unpaid rent, the landlord may terminate if rent is not paid within the time stated in a written notice of not less than 10 calendar days after receipt (HRS 521-68(a) as amended by Act 278, SLH 2025, effective 2026-02-05; the notice must also include the mediation language in 521-68(b); deemed received on posting, or 2 business days after postmark if mailed). A notice of termination made to evade the rent-increase notice rules is void (521-71(f)).
rent_increase_notice: Month-to-month tenancy: the landlord may not increase rent without written notice given 45 consecutive days before the effective date (HRS 521-21(d)). Tenancy shorter than month-to-month: 15 consecutive days' written notice (521-21(e)). A termination notice given to evade these requirements is void (521-71(f)). The retaliation section also bars demanding a rent increase after a good-faith complaint or repair request (521-74(a)).
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No statewide rent control or rent-increase cap found in ch. 521 (a 2026 rent-cap bill, SB2539, is reported dead).
retaliation_rule: While the tenant keeps tendering the usual rent, the landlord may not bring an action for possession, force the tenant out, demand a rent increase, or decrease services after the tenant (1) complained in good faith to the health department, landlord, building department, consumer protection office or other agency about a health-law or ch. 521 violation, (2) an agency filed a complaint or notice of violation, or (3) the tenant in good faith requested repairs under 521-63 or 521-64 (HRS 521-74(a)). Exceptions include waste, nuisance or illegal use; good-faith recovery for the landlord's or immediate family's own abode, or to alter, remodel or demolish; conditions caused by the tenant; a health department certification of compliance; a good-faith contract of sale; and a periodic-tenancy termination notice given before the complaint (521-74(b)). Rent may still be raised for property tax or operating cost increases, capital improvements, comparable market rent, or after a compliance certification (521-74(d)). The tenant may recover damages and costs including attorney's fees (521-74(c)). No time-based presumption found.

deposit_max: No statutory cap on the amount of a security deposit found in Idaho Code 6-321. Any amount a tenant deposits for a purpose other than rent counts as a security deposit (6-321(1)). The landlord may not keep any part of it for normal wear and tear (6-321(1)). Other titles of the Idaho Code were not searched.
deposit_interest: No interest requirement found in 6-321. A separate-account requirement exists only where a third-party manager manages the residential premises for the landlord (6-321(4)); it does not apply to the property owner itself, a real estate licensee, and certain related entities.
late_fee_rule: Fees charged to a residential tenant, including fees for late payment of rent, must be reasonable (55-305(1)). An owner may not charge a fee, fine, assessment, interest or other cost above the amount agreed in the rental agreement, or one not in the rental agreement unless the agreement is oral, or the written agreement is changed by 30 days' written notice (55-305(2)). Applies to agreements entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2023 (55-305(3)). No fixed dollar or percentage cap and no statutory grace period found.
entry_notice: No statute found in Idaho Code Title 6 ch. 3 or Title 55 ch. 2-3 that sets landlord entry rights or an advance-notice period; entry terms come from the lease. Other titles were not searched.
entry_citation: Idaho Code Title 6 ch. 3; Title 55 ch. 2-3 (no provision found)
month_to_month_tenant_notice: A tenant ending a tenancy at will must give the landlord written notice stating the date of vacating, which must be not less than one (1) month after the date of the notice (55-208(2)).
month_to_month_landlord_notice: A landlord ending a tenancy at will must give the tenant written notice, served in the manner prescribed by the code of civil procedure, to remove from the premises within a period of not less than one (1) month, specified in the notice (55-208(1)). Separately, for unpaid rent the landlord must serve a 3-day written notice to pay or vacate (6-303(2)); for other lease breaches a 3-day notice to perform or vacate (6-303(3)).
rent_increase_notice: For leases of residential property the landlord must give the tenant written notice of any increase in the amount of rent charged, or of the landlord's intention not to renew the lease, at least thirty (30) days before the nonrenewal or before the rent increase takes effect (55-304(2)). For month-to-month leases the landlord may otherwise change lease terms by written notice at least 15 days before the end of the month, effective at month end (55-304(1)); subsection (2) applies 'notwithstanding' (1) to residential rent increases.
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No state rent cap found. A local government may not enact, maintain or enforce an ordinance or resolution that would regulate rent, fees or deposits charged for leasing private residential property (55-306).

deposit_max: No statewide cap.
deposit_interest: Landlords with 25+ units in one building or contiguous complex must pay interest on deposits held more than 6 months (765 ILCS 715). Chicago (RLTO) requires interest on all deposits.
late_fee_rule: No statewide Illinois statute found that caps residential late fees or sets a rent grace period: neither the Landlord and Tenant Act (765 ILCS 705) nor the Security Deposit Return Act (765 ILCS 710) has a late-fee provision, and the fee-transparency bill HB 3564 (104th General Assembly, adding 765 ILCS 705/35; final effective date not confirmed) does not cap late fees. Any late fee comes from the lease. Local rules can differ: Chicago's Residential Landlord and Tenant Ordinance sets its own late-fee limit. The eviction article (735 ILCS 5/9-102 to 9-218) also has no residential late-fee provision. Other Illinois statutes were not searched.
late_fee_citation: 765 ILCS 705 and 765 ILCS 710 (no late-fee provision found); HB 3564 (765 ILCS 705/35)
entry_notice: No statewide statute; Chicago RLTO requires 2 days' notice.
month_to_month_tenant_notice: 30 days
month_to_month_landlord_notice: 30 days
rent_increase_notice: No statewide notice statute beyond ending a periodic tenancy.
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No; local rent control is preempted (50 ILCS 825).
retaliation_rule: Retaliation against tenants who complain to authorities or exercise legal rights is prohibited.

deposit_max: No statutory cap on the amount of a security deposit found in IC 32-31-3. The term includes required prepayment of rent beyond the first full rental period and other refundable amounts (IC 32-31-3-9). A deposit may be used only for actual damage beyond ordinary wear and tear, unpaid rent (including rent due for premature termination), last month's rent if agreed in writing, and unpaid utility or sewer charges the tenant owed under the lease (IC 32-31-3-13).
deposit_interest: No interest or separate-account requirement found in IC 32-31-3.
late_fee_rule: No provision on residential late fees found in IC 32-31 (the whole article was searched). Any late fee must come from the lease. Cities and towns may not regulate landlord fees by ordinance (IC 32-31-1-20(c)(7)). Other titles of the Indiana Code were not searched.
entry_notice: The landlord must give the tenant reasonable written or oral notice of intent to enter and may enter only at reasonable times; no fixed number of hours is set. The landlord may not abuse the right of entry or use it to harass. Entry without notice is allowed in an emergency that threatens the safety of occupants or the landlord's property, and without consent under a court order or if the unit is abandoned. The tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent for inspections, repairs, services or showings. A landlord may not change the locks or cut off electricity, gas, water or other essential services to exclude or pressure a tenant (except for emergencies, good-faith repairs or necessary construction).
month_to_month_tenant_notice: The statute does not separately state a tenant notice period for ending a month-to-month tenancy (IC 32-31-1-1 refers to notice 'delivered to the tenant'). In practice one month's written notice is used, but this is not stated for tenants.
month_to_month_landlord_notice: One month's written notice delivered to the tenant to end a tenancy at will (IC 32-31-1-1); for a periodic tenancy of 3 months or less, notice equal to the interval between periods (IC 32-31-1-4), i.e. one month for monthly rent. For unpaid rent, not less than 10 days' notice unless the parties agreed otherwise or the tenant pays in full before it ends (IC 32-31-1-6). A protected crime victim may end a lease on 30 days' written notice with the documents required by IC 32-31-9-12.
rent_increase_notice: Unless a written rental agreement provides otherwise, the landlord must give at least 30 days' written notice before modifying the rental agreement (IC 32-31-5-4). The statute speaks of modifying the agreement, not specifically of rent.
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No statewide rent cap found, and cities and towns may not regulate rental rates unless the General Assembly authorises it (government-subsidised property excepted) (IC 32-31-1-20(b)).
retaliation_rule: A landlord may not raise rent, cut or interfere with services, or bring or threaten an eviction or possession action in response to protected activity: complaining to a code-enforcement agency about a health or safety violation, written complaint to the landlord about a violation of the entry or habitability duties, suing the landlord under ch. 6 or 8, joining a tenant organisation, or testifying against the landlord. Exceptions include not renewing at term end, raising rent to comparable market rent, equal service cuts, unpaid rent not cured, tenant-caused violations, and good-faith owner use or demolition. No time-based presumption.

deposit_max: 2 months' rent. The deposit must be held in a federally insured bank, savings and loan or credit union account, not mixed with the landlord's own money.
deposit_interest: No for the first five years of a tenancy: interest earned in that period belongs to the landlord.
late_fee_rule: Rent up to $700/month: late fee capped at $12 per day and $60 per month. Rent over $700/month: capped at $20 per day and $100 per month.
entry_notice: At least 24 hours' notice and entry only at reasonable times, except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable. Entry without consent is allowed in an emergency. The tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to inspect, repair or show the unit; the landlord may not abuse access or use it to harass the tenant.
month_to_month_tenant_notice: 30 days' written notice before the periodic rental date named in the notice (10 days for week-to-week)
month_to_month_landlord_notice: 30 days' written notice before the periodic rental date named in the notice (10 days for week-to-week)
rent_increase_notice: Written notice at least 30 days before the increase takes effect, and the increase cannot take effect before the current lease term (or its renewal/extension) ends.
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No; Iowa cities may not adopt or enforce limits on the amount of rent for private residential property (Iowa Code § 364.3(9)).
retaliation_rule: Landlord may not raise rent, cut services, or bring or threaten an eviction because the tenant complained to a housing-code agency, complained to the landlord about required repairs, or joined a tenants' union. A good-faith complaint within the prior year creates a presumption of retaliation. The tenant can recover actual damages and reasonable attorney fees.

deposit_max: 1 month's rent for an unfurnished unit; 1.5 months' rent if the tenant uses the landlord's furniture; plus up to half a month's rent extra if pets are allowed.
late_fee_rule: No statewide rule found: the Kansas Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (K.S.A. 58-2540 to 58-2573) has no provision capping late fees or requiring a grace period, so any late fee comes from the lease (58-2545(a)). Rent is payable at the time and place agreed, by default at the beginning of each month (58-2545(c)), and the landlord may end the lease if rent is unpaid 3 days after written notice (58-2564(b)). A court may refuse to enforce an unconscionable lease term (58-2544(a)). Other Kansas statutes were not searched.
entry_notice: Reasonable notice and entry at reasonable hours (no fixed number of hours in the statute), to inspect, repair, supply services or show the unit. Entry without consent is allowed in an extreme hazard involving potential loss of life or severe property damage. The landlord may not abuse access or use it to harass the tenant.
month_to_month_tenant_notice: 30 days' written notice, ending on a rent-paying date (15 days for tenants in military service under military orders)
month_to_month_landlord_notice: 30 days' written notice, ending on a rent-paying date
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No; cities and counties may not enact or enforce rent control on private residential property (state preemption).
retaliation_rule: Landlord may not retaliate by raising rent or cutting services because the tenant complained to a housing-code agency, complained to the landlord about required repairs, or joined a tenants' union. A good-faith increase to cover higher costs (taxes, utility rates) is allowed if the lease permits it.

deposit_max: No statewide cap. Under the URLTA (where adopted): deposit must be kept in a separate account used only for deposits, and the landlord must give signed move-in and move-out damage lists, or they cannot keep any of the deposit.
late_fee_rule: No provision capping residential late fees or requiring a grace period was found in KRS chapter 383 (including the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, KRS 383.505 to 383.715), so any late fee depends on the lease. The URLTA applies only where a city, county or urban-county government has adopted it (KRS 383.500); where it applies, rent is due without demand at the beginning of each month unless the lease says otherwise (KRS 383.565(2)). Other Kentucky statutes were not searched.
late_fee_citation: KRS 383.565(2); KRS 383.500 (KRS 383 searched; no late-fee provision)
entry_notice: At least 2 days' notice, except in an emergency or where impracticable (URLTA areas).
month_to_month_tenant_notice: 30 days' written notice before the periodic rental date (URLTA areas)
month_to_month_landlord_notice: 30 days' written notice before the periodic rental date (URLTA areas); elsewhere, one month's written notice to end a tenancy at will (KRS 383.195)
retaliation_rule: Landlord may not raise rent, cut services, or sue/threaten eviction because the tenant complained to a code agency or the landlord, or joined a tenants' union; a complaint within 1 year before the act creates a presumption of retaliation (URLTA areas).

deposit_max: No statutory cap. The landlord may keep only what is reasonably necessary to remedy the tenant's default or unreasonable wear to the premises (R.S. 9:3251(A)).
deposit_interest: false
late_fee_rule: No statewide cap, grace period or notice rule for residential late fees was found in Louisiana's lease law (Civil Code arts. 2668-2729, R.S. 9:3251-3261), so a late fee comes from the lease and is treated as stipulated damages under the Civil Code: the landlord need not prove actual loss (art. 2009), the fee applies only once the tenant is in default (art. 2010), and a court may modify it only if it is so manifestly unreasonable as to be contrary to public policy (art. 2012). The 5% / $25 limit in R.S. 9:3314 applies to leases of movable property such as vehicles, not homes. Other statutes were not searched.
late_fee_citation: La. Civ. Code arts. 2005, 2009, 2010, 2012; no residential late-fee provision in La. Civ. Code arts. 2668-2729 or La. R.S. 9:3251-3261
month_to_month_tenant_notice: Written notice at least 10 calendar days before the end of the month.
month_to_month_landlord_notice: Written notice at least 10 calendar days before the end of the month.

deposit_max: 2 months' rent. At move-in the landlord may not require more than the first full month's rent, the security deposit and any properly disclosed mandatory recurring fee (§ 6022-A). The deposit may not be commingled with the landlord's assets: it must be held in a bank or other financial institution account beyond the reach of the landlord's creditors, and on request the landlord must tell the tenant the institution and account number (§ 6038). Exemption: the security-deposit chapter does not apply to a unit in a building of 5 or fewer units where one unit is occupied by the landlord (§ 6037(2)).
deposit_interest: No interest requirement in ch. 710-A.
late_fee_rule: Rent is late only if not paid within 15 days of the due date, and the late fee may not exceed 4% of one month's rent. No late fee may be charged unless the tenant was told in writing, when the rental agreement was made, that a fee of up to 4% may be charged.
entry_notice: Reasonable notice and entry only at reasonable times, except in an emergency or where notice is impracticable; 24 hours is presumed reasonable. Unlawful, unreasonable or harassing entry lets the tenant recover actual damages or $250, whichever is greater. Any waiver of these rights is void.
month_to_month_tenant_notice: At least 30 days' written notice (tenancy at will)
month_to_month_landlord_notice: At least 30 days' written notice (tenancy at will); 7 days for specified causes such as rent 7+ days in arrears or substantial damage. The notice must tell the tenant they have the right to contest the termination in court.
rent_increase_notice: At least 45 days' written notice before rent or a mandatory recurring fee is increased; at least 75 days' notice if the increase (or several increases within 12 months) totals 10% or more. Rent may not be increased while the unit violates the warranty of habitability (unless the tenant caused the violation). Waivers are void.
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No statewide cap on the amount of rent; state law regulates notice and bars increases while the unit is uninhabitable.
retaliation_rule: An eviction action is presumed retaliatory if, within the 6 months before it was filed, the tenant asserted rights under the rent-increase, habitability or fee statutes, made a good-faith code complaint to an enforcement body, or made a good-faith written repair request to the landlord.

deposit_max: 1 month's rent per unit (since Oct 1, 2024); up to 2 months only if the tenant qualified for utility assistance through the Department of Human Services, the lease requires paying utilities directly to the landlord, and both agree in writing. Overcharge: tenant may recover up to 3x the excess plus attorney fees.
deposit_interest: Yes: simple interest at the greater of the 1-year U.S. Treasury yield rate or 1.5% per year, only on deposits of $50 or more held at least 6 months.
late_fee_rule: Lease may not set a late fee above 5% of the unpaid rent (for weekly rent: max $3 per week and $12 per month).
month_to_month_tenant_notice: 30 days (oral or written notice before end of the tenancy; in Baltimore City written notice).
month_to_month_landlord_notice: 60 days written notice (month-to-month or lease term over 1 week); 90 days for year-to-year; shorter 30/60 days only in a foreclosure situation.
rent_increase_notice: Written notice at least 90 days ahead for tenancies longer than 1 month, 60 days for 1 week to 1 month; sent by first-class mail with certificate of mailing (or e-delivery if the tenant elects).
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No statewide cap found in Title 8; § 8-209 only regulates notice and does not displace local laws.
retaliation_rule: Landlord may not sue or threaten to sue for possession, arbitrarily raise rent, cut services or end a periodic tenancy because of a good-faith complaint (to the landlord or a public agency), a lawsuit, tenant-organization activity, or someone summoning police/emergency services; damages up to 3 months' rent plus attorney fees. Protection requires the tenant to be current on rent (unless lawfully withholding) and covers actions within 6 months of the complaint/lawsuit.

deposit_max: One month's rent. At or before the start of the tenancy the landlord (or its agent) may require only: rent for the first full month, rent for the last full month at the same rate, a security deposit equal to the first month's rent, and the purchase and installation cost of a key and lock. After the tenancy begins the landlord may not demand rent in advance beyond the current month or a larger deposit. The deposit stays the tenant's property: it must be held in a separate interest-bearing account in a bank located in Massachusetts, out of reach of the landlord's creditors, and the tenant must get a receipt within 30 days naming the bank, its location and the account number (failure entitles the tenant to immediate return). The landlord must give a signed receipt when taking the deposit and, within 10 days after the tenancy starts (or on receipt of the deposit, if later), a separate signed written statement of the unit's condition with a prescribed notice; the tenant has 15 days to return it with a list of any other damage. The landlord must also keep records of deposits for two years.
deposit_interest: Yes. If the deposit is held a year or longer, 5% per year or the lesser amount the bank actually paid, paid to the tenant each year with a statement naming the bank, account number and amount (any accrued interest is due within 30 days if the tenancy ends before the anniversary). Interest on prepaid last month's rent is also owed at 5% or the lesser bank rate.
late_fee_rule: A lease may not impose any interest or penalty for failure to pay rent until 30 days after the rent was due.
entry_notice: Massachusetts has no statute setting a notice period for entry. Section 15B(1)(a) bars a lease from giving the landlord a right to enter before the lease ends except to inspect, make repairs or show the unit to a prospective tenant, purchaser or mortgagee (or its agents). The landlord may also enter under a court order, if the premises appear abandoned, or to inspect in the last 30 days of the tenancy after either side has given notice to end it, to assess damage that might be deducted from the deposit. Interfering with the tenant's quiet enjoyment, or regaining possession by force without a court process, is a crime (fine of $25 to $300 or up to 6 months in jail) and the tenant may recover actual and consequential damages or three months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees; any lease waiver is void.
month_to_month_tenant_notice: Notice in writing at least equal to the interval between rent payment days or 30 days, whichever is longer (monthly rent: 30 days). The statute says either party may end a tenancy at will with that notice.
month_to_month_landlord_notice: Same: written notice at least equal to the rent interval or 30 days, whichever is longer, and the tenant cannot be dispossessed before it expires. For non-payment of rent, 14 days' written notice to quit is enough, but a tenant at will who has not received a similar notice in the prior 12 months can stop the termination by paying all rent due within 10 days after receiving it, and the notice must contain a statutory statement of that right. A lease provision waiving these notices is void (§ 15A). A tenancy at will is not ended by a sale, transfer or foreclosure.
rent_increase_notice: Massachusetts has no separate statute setting a rent-increase notice period. Under § 12 a tenancy at will can be changed only by ending it with written notice (rent interval or 30 days, whichever is longer), and the statute expressly allows that notice to include an offer of a new tenancy on different terms. Rent cannot be raised during a fixed lease term unless the lease allows it (lease terms not verified here). A landlord may not increase rent as a reprisal for a tenant's protected activity; a rent increase within 6 months after the activity is presumed to be a reprisal (§ 18). A landlord may not raise rent because a tenant made repairs under c. 111 § 127L, except by court order.
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: Rent control is prohibited statewide by the Massachusetts Rent Control Prohibition Act (c. 40P), which bars rent-control schemes except voluntary ones.
retaliation_rule: A landlord may not threaten or take reprisals against a tenant for reporting a code violation to the board of health or other enforcement body, complaining in writing to the landlord, suing or seeking relief under a housing law, or organizing or joining a tenants' union. The landlord is liable for actual damages or one to three months' rent, whichever is greater, plus costs and attorney's fees. A notice terminating the tenancy (other than for non-payment of rent), a rent increase or a substantial change in lease terms within 6 months after the tenant's protected activity is presumed to be a reprisal, rebuttable only by clear and convincing evidence of an independent justification. Retaliation is also a defense to eviction (c. 239 § 2A, same 6-month presumption). Any lease waiver is void.

deposit_max: 1.5 months' rent (554.602). The deposit must be kept in a regulated financial institution, or the landlord must instead post a cash or surety bond with the Secretary of State covering all deposits (554.604). Before it may require a deposit, the landlord must give the tenant a written notice, within 14 days after the tenant takes possession, of the landlord's name and address, the name and address of the financial institution or surety, and the tenant's duty to give a forwarding address within 4 days after moving out, with that warning in bold 12-point type (554.603). The landlord must give the tenant two blank copies of a move-in inventory checklist and a termination checklist is required at move-out; the tenant has 7 days after getting possession to return the move-in checklist (554.608). The deposit may be used only for actual damage beyond normal use, unpaid rent, rent due for early termination, and unpaid tenant utility bills (554.607).
deposit_interest: No. The Michigan act does not require interest on the deposit.
late_fee_rule: No Michigan statute found that caps or limits residential late fees or sets a grace period. Check the lease. Since September 21, 2026, a lease that allows more than one way to pay rent must include at least one method with no added charge or fee, and may not charge an extra fee on all allowed payment methods (554.633(1)(o), added by 2026 PA 103).
entry_notice: No Michigan statute found that sets a notice period or hours for landlord entry. Unlawful interference with a tenant's possession includes use of force, changing locks without providing keys, or removing doors, windows or locks, but a landlord's temporary interference needed for repairs or inspection 'as provided by law' is not unlawful. Check the lease. A tenant who is wrongfully excluded can recover actual damages or $200 per occurrence, whichever is greater (600.2918(2), (3)(b)).
month_to_month_tenant_notice: A month-to-month tenancy (an estate at will) can be ended by either party with 1 month's notice. If rent is payable at intervals shorter than 3 months, notice equal to the interval between rent payments is enough. The notice does not need to match the rental period dates, and it ends the tenancy at the end of a period equal to the payment interval (554.134(1)). A year-to-year tenancy ends 1 year after service of a notice to quit given at any time (554.134(3)).
month_to_month_landlord_notice: Same 1-month notice rule applies to the landlord (554.134(1)). For unpaid rent the landlord may give a 7-day notice to quit, and may begin summary proceedings if the tenant does not pay or leave within 7 days of a written demand (554.134(2); 600.5714(1)(a)). A 24-hour notice is allowed for drug-related lease terminations when a police report was filed (554.134(4); 600.5714(1)(b)), and a 7-day notice after a tenant or household member caused or threatened physical injury (600.5714(1)(e)). A landlord may not use force, lock-outs or utility shut-offs to remove a tenant: the tenant can recover the greater of actual damages or $200 per occurrence, or 3 times actual damages or $200 for forcible ejection (600.2918(1), (2)). Landlords of 5 or more rental units may not deny or end a tenancy based on source of income (554.601c). A tenant who has lived in the unit more than 13 months can end a lease with 60 days' written notice on becoming eligible for subsidized senior citizen housing or being certified by a physician as unable to live independently, if the rental agreement so provides (554.601a). A tenant with a reasonable apprehension of danger from domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking can be released from rent obligation by certified-mail notice with documentation (554.601b).
rent_increase_notice: No Michigan statute found that requires advance notice of a rent increase for a month-to-month tenancy. A landlord cannot change a lease term mid-lease without the tenant's written consent, except that a lease may allow changes on at least 30 days' written notice for legal requirements, safety rules, or rent increases covering higher property taxes, electricity/heat/water/sewer charges, or liability, fire or workers' compensation insurance premiums (554.633(1)(l)). A termination or rent increase made as a penalty for asserting legal rights is a defense to eviction (600.5720(1)(a), (e)).
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No statewide rent control. Local governments may not enact, maintain or enforce rent control on private residential property (123.411(2)); they may adopt voluntary incentives to increase affordable housing supply (123.411(4)).
retaliation_rule: A court may not enter a judgment for possession if the termination was intended primarily as a penalty for the tenant's attempt to secure or enforce rights under the lease or law, for a complaint to a government authority about health or safety code violations, or as retribution for a lawful act arising out of the tenancy, including tenant organization membership. If the tenant shows they took official action (through a court or government agency) within 90 days before the eviction case began and it was not dismissed or denied, a presumption of retaliation arises that the landlord must rebut by a preponderance of the evidence. If the action was more than 90 days earlier or ended against the tenant, the presumption is against the tenant (600.5720(2)). The statute is framed as a defense to a possession judgment, not a general ban on retaliation.

deposit_max: No statutory cap on the amount.
deposit_interest: Yes: 1% simple, noncompounded interest per year (amounts under $1 excluded).
late_fee_rule: Only if agreed in writing, and the agreement must say when the fee is imposed; capped at 8% of the overdue rent payment. Federally subsidized tenancies may follow a conflicting federal fee schedule; for assisted tenancies the fee is calculated only on the tenant's portion of rent.
entry_notice: Only for a reasonable business purpose and after a good-faith effort to give at least 24 hours' notice specifying a time or window; entry only between 8:00 a.m. and 8:00 p.m. unless agreed. No notice needed when immediate entry is necessary for safety/emergency reasons. The tenant cannot be required to waive the notice right as a condition of the lease.
month_to_month_tenant_notice: Written notice at least as long as the interval between rent due dates (or three months, whichever is less)
month_to_month_landlord_notice: Written notice at least as long as the interval between rent due dates (or three months, whichever is less)
rent_increase_notice: No general statutory notice period for rent increases. But if a lease gives the landlord a different notice period than the tenant, the landlord's notice of a rent increase (or to quit / non-renewal) may not be shorter than the notice the lease requires from the tenant; this cannot be waived.
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No; cities and counties may control rents only through an ordinance or charter amendment approved in a general election (Minn. Stat. § 471.9996).
retaliation_rule: A landlord may not evict, increase obligations or decrease services as a penalty for a tenant's good-faith complaint or for enforcing lease or legal rights. If the action comes within 90 days of the complaint/act, the landlord bears the burden of proving it was not retaliatory.

deposit_max: No statutory cap on the amount of a security deposit found in the Act (89-8-1 to 89-8-45 read in full). The deposit rule covers any payment or deposit of money whose primary function is to secure performance of the rental agreement, other than a payment or deposit (including advance rent) made to secure execution of the rental agreement (89-8-21(1)). The landlord may keep only amounts reasonably necessary to remedy the tenant's defaults in rent, repair damage caused by the tenant (excluding ordinary wear and tear), clean the premises at the end of the tenancy, or cover other reasonable and necessary expenses caused by the tenant's default (89-8-21(3)).
deposit_interest: No interest or separate-account requirement found in 89-8-21; the statute only says the deposit is held by the landlord for the tenant and the tenant's claim is prior to the claims of the landlord's creditors (89-8-21(2)).
late_fee_rule: No provision found in the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act that caps, limits or requires a grace period for late fees. The Act defines 'rent' to include any late fees required to be paid under the rental agreement by a defaulting tenant (89-8-7(1)(k)), so a late fee is a matter of the lease. Other titles of the Mississippi Code were not searched.
entry_notice: No provision found: the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (89-8-1 to 89-8-45) contains no section on landlord entry or access to a rented unit, and states no notice period. Other titles of the Mississippi Code were not searched.
month_to_month_tenant_notice: At least 30 days' written notice before the termination date (89-8-19(3)); a week-to-week tenancy needs at least 7 days' written notice (89-8-19(2)). If the rental agreement fixes no definite term the tenancy is week-to-week for a tenant who pays weekly rent and month-to-month in all other cases (89-8-19(1)).
month_to_month_landlord_notice: At least 30 days' written notice before the termination date (89-8-19(3)); 7 days for week-to-week (89-8-19(2)). No notice is required when the landlord or tenant has committed a substantial violation of the rental agreement or the Act that materially affects health or safety (89-8-19(4)). For breach by the tenant, the landlord may give written notice (or email/text if the tenant agreed in writing) that the agreement ends not less than 14 days after receipt if the breach is not remedied within a reasonable time of at most 14 days (89-8-13(3)); for nonpayment of rent the notice may give 3 days to pay before the agreement terminates (89-8-13(5)(a)). After a fixed-term agreement expires, the landlord may give a hold-over notice that eviction proceedings will start no earlier than 3 days after the notice (89-8-17(2)).
rent_increase_notice: No provision found requiring advance notice of a rent increase. The only rent-increase text is in 89-8-17(2): after a rental agreement expires, the landlord may demand an increase in rent if the landlord's actions did not have the dominant purpose of retaliation against the tenant for actions authorized under the Act and the landlord received written notice of each condition that was the subject of the tenant's actions.
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No statewide rent control provision found in the Act. Other titles of the Mississippi Code were not searched.
retaliation_rule: No general anti-retaliation section found in the Act. The only retaliation text is in 89-8-17(2): the landlord may demand a rent increase after a rental agreement expires only if the landlord's actions did not have the dominant purpose of retaliation against the tenant for actions authorized under the Act and the landlord received written notice of each condition that was the subject of the tenant's actions. The Act also imposes a general duty of good faith on the landlord's termination, nonrenewal and removal of a tenant (89-8-9).

deposit_max: Two months' rent. Must be held in a federally insured bank, credit union or depository institution; interest earned belongs to the landlord. Pet deposits are not counted as 'security deposit'.
deposit_interest: false
late_fee_rule: No statewide cap, grace period or other rule on residential rent late fees was found in Missouri's landlord-tenant statutes (RSMo chapters 441 and 535, all sections read), so any late fee depends on the lease. Rent not paid at the time agreed by the parties is what triggers the landlord's action for possession (RSMo 535.010). In an unpaid-rent case the landlord may also claim other unpaid sums owed under the lease (such as late fees), but those sums are not rent for chapter 535 and a judgment for them does not by itself entitle the landlord to possession (RSMo 535.020). Other Missouri statutes were not searched.
late_fee_citation: RSMo chs. 441 and 535 (no late-fee provision found); RSMo 535.010; RSMo 535.020; RSMo 441.043(1)
month_to_month_tenant_notice: Written notice; tenancy ends on a rent-paying date at least one month after the landlord receives it
month_to_month_landlord_notice: Written notice; tenancy ends on a rent-paying date at least one month after the tenant receives it
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: Cities and counties may not enact or enforce rent control ordinances (with narrow exceptions for subsidized/public property).

deposit_max: No statutory cap found in chapter 70-25. Any deposit the lease requires counts as a security deposit, and a fee or charge for cleaning and damages, however labelled, is presumed to be one (§ 70-25-101(4)). Any lease term contrary to chapter 70-25, and any tenant waiver of it, is invalid (§ 70-25-103).
deposit_interest: No interest requirement in chapter 70-25.
late_fee_citation: MCA chs. 70-24 and 70-25 (no late-fee cap or grace period found; § 70-24-103(14) defines "rent" to include "late fees, or other charges as agreed on in the rental agreement"; § 70-25-201(1) lets a landlord deduct 'late charges' and 'penalties due under lease provisions' from the deposit, and § 70-24-201(4) bars an additional fee based on rent payment type except to recoup an electronic bank fee for electronic payment; other titles were not searched)
entry_notice: Except in an emergency or where it is impracticable, the landlord must give at least 24 hours' notice of intent to enter and may enter only at reasonable times; the landlord may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant. The tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to entry for inspection, repairs, services or showings. The notice can be given as provided in § 70-24-108 or by conspicuously posting it on the main entry door. Emergency entry needs no consent. If the landlord enters unlawfully or unreasonably, or makes repeated harassing demands, the tenant may get an injunction or terminate the lease, and recover actual damages (§ 70-24-410).
month_to_month_tenant_notice: At least 30 days' written notice before the termination date given in the notice (month-to-month); at least 7 days' written notice for week-to-week.
month_to_month_landlord_notice: Same: at least 30 days' written notice for month-to-month; 7 days for week-to-week. For nonpayment, the landlord may terminate if the tenant fails to pay within 3 days after written notice of nonpayment and intent to terminate (§ 70-24-422(2)). For other lease breaches the notice period is 14 days (3 days for an unauthorized pet, unauthorized occupants or verbal abuse of the landlord) (§ 70-24-422(1)). A landlord is not bound by § 70-24-422 if it elects to use the 30-day notice (§ 70-24-422(7)). A fixed-term lease that runs out with no agreed extension and no 30-day notice from either side continues month-to-month (§ 70-24-205).
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No rent-increase notice requirement and no rent control provision found in chapter 70-24 (other titles not searched). A landlord may adopt a new rule that substantially modifies the tenant's bargain only on 30 days' written notice for month-to-month tenancies (§ 70-24-311(3)). Increasing rent in retaliation for a protected complaint is barred (§ 70-24-431).
retaliation_rule: A landlord may not retaliate by increasing rent, decreasing services, or bringing or threatening an action for possession after the tenant (a) complained of a health-and-safety code violation to a government agency, (b) complained in writing to the landlord of a violation of § 70-24-303 (habitability), or (c) organized or joined a tenants' union. A complaint within 6 months before the alleged retaliation creates a rebuttable presumption of retaliation (not if the tenant complained after notice of a proposed rent increase or reduced services). The tenant gets the remedies of § 70-24-411 and a defense to a possession action. The landlord may still seek possession if the tenant caused the violation, is in default in rent, or compliance requires work that would deprive the tenant of the unit.

deposit_max: One month's periodic rent; a pet deposit of up to one-fourth of one month's rent may also be demanded (Neb. Rev. Stat. 76-1416(1)); the cap does not apply to housing agencies under the Nebraska Housing Agency Act.
deposit_interest: No interest or separate-account requirement found in 76-1416.
late_fee_rule: No provision on residential late fees found in 76-1401 to 76-1449 of the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. Any late fee must come from the lease. Other chapters of Nebraska law were not searched.
entry_notice: Except in an emergency or if impracticable, the landlord must give at least 24 hours' written notice of intent to enter, stating the purpose and a reasonable period for the entry, and may enter only at reasonable times (76-1423(3)). Landlord may enter without consent in an emergency (76-1423(2)); the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent (76-1423(1)).
month_to_month_tenant_notice: At least 30 days' written notice before the periodic rental date specified in the notice (76-1437(2)); week-to-week tenancy: 7 days (76-1437(1)).
month_to_month_landlord_notice: Same: at least 30 days' written notice before the periodic rental date specified in the notice (76-1437(2)). For unpaid rent, the landlord may terminate if the tenant does not pay within 7 calendar days after written notice of nonpayment and intent to terminate (76-1431(2)).
rent_increase_notice: No statute on the notice required for a rent increase found in 76-1401 to 76-1449. A month-to-month tenancy can be ended on 30 days' notice (76-1437(2)); retaliatory rent increases are prohibited (76-1439).
retaliation_rule: A landlord may not retaliate by increasing rent, decreasing services, or bringing or threatening an action for possession after the tenant complains to a government agency about a code violation materially affecting health and safety, or organizes or joins a tenants' union. Exceptions: violation caused by the tenant, tenant in rent default, or compliance requiring alteration or demolition that would deprive the tenant of the unit. No time-based presumption.

deposit_max: 3 months' periodic rent total (deposit, surety bond and last month's rent combined).
late_fee_rule: Must be reasonable, set out in the rental agreement, and no more than 5% of the periodic rent; in tenancies longer than week to week, no late fee until at least 3 calendar days after rent is due; the maximum cannot be increased based on a prior late fee.
entry_notice: At least 24 hours' notice, at reasonable times during normal business hours (unless tenant consents otherwise); no notice needed in an emergency.
month_to_month_landlord_notice: At least 30 days' notice for monthly and other periodic tenancies (7 days week-to-week). A tenant aged 60+ or with a disability can ask in writing for 30 more days (not for week-to-week tenancies).
rent_increase_notice: Written notice 60 days before the first increased payment (30 days if the periodic tenancy is under 1 month).
rent_increase_statewide_rent_control: No statewide cap on the amount found; the statute only requires notice.
retaliation_rule: Landlord may not retaliate (end or refuse to renew tenancy, raise rent, cut services, or threaten eviction) because a tenant made a good-faith code complaint, organized a tenants' group, or used habitability remedies.

deposit_max: A landlord may not demand or receive a security deposit above one month's rent or $100, whichever is greater (RSA 540-A:6, I(a)); if the lease calls for quarterly or less frequent rent, a deposit taken in addition to the first rent payment may not exceed one month's rent. 'Security deposit' means all funds in excess of the monthly rent transferred from tenant to landlord for any purpose (540-A:5, II). The landlord must promptly give a signed receipt stating the amount and where the deposit is held (not required if paid by personal, bank or government/nonprofit check) and a written list of unit conditions needing repair, which the tenant may note within 5 days of occupancy (540-A:6, I(b)-(c)). Deposits are held in trust, not mingled with the landlord's own money (a single trust account of all deposits at a NH bank is allowed; a NH surety bond posted with the city/town clerk is an alternative) (540-A:6, II). Landlord definition (540-A:5, I): a person who rents a single-family residence and owns no other rental property, or who rents units in an owner-occupied building of 5 units or less, is NOT a 'landlord' for this deposit subdivision, except for a unit occupied by someone aged 60+.
deposit_interest: Yes, after one year: a landlord who holds a deposit for one year or longer must pay interest at the rate paid on regular savings accounts at a NH bank, savings and loan or credit union (actual interest earned, pro rata, if deposits are pooled), counted from the date the deposit was received (or September 13, 1977, if later) (RSA 540-A:6, IV(a)). A tenant may request accrued interest every 3 years, 30 days before the end of the year's tenancy; the landlord must pay within 15 days after the year ends (540-A:6, IV(c)). On request the landlord must give the bank name, account number, amount on deposit and interest rate (540-A:6, IV(b)).
late_fee_rule: No provision on residential late fees found in the sections read (RSA 540-A:3-8, 540:2, 540:3). Not every RSA title was searched; any late fee therefore comes from the lease. (NH does regulate a different fee: an application/renewal fee must be disclosed in writing beforehand and, if the unit is not rented to that applicant, anything beyond actual documented screening cost and reasonable administrative cost must be returned within 30 days - RSA 540-A:3, VIII, eff. 2025-01-01.)
late_fee_citation: RSA 540-A:3, VIII (application fees only); no late-fee provision found
entry_notice: A landlord may not willfully enter the tenant's premises without prior consent, other than to make emergency repairs (RSA 540-A:3, IV). Without consent the landlord may enter only for emergency repairs (including emergency evaluation/remediation of an insect or rodent infestation within 72 hours of first notice) or under a court order (540-A:3, IV-a, V-d). A tenant may not willfully refuse the landlord access to make necessary repairs or perform other reasonable and lawful functions of rental-property ownership 'at a reasonable time after notice which is adequate under the circumstances' (540-A:3, V). No fixed number of hours' notice is set, except 48 hours' written notice to inspect for bed bugs next to an infested unit (540-A:3, V-b) and at least 72 hours for written preparation instructions before pest remediation (V-c). A landlord may not willfully cut utilities (water, heat, electricity, gas etc., except temporary interruption during actual repairs or emergencies) or deny the tenant access/possession other than through judicial process (540-A:3, I-III). A landlord who vacated-tenant property must store it with reasonable care for 7 days (540-A:3, VII). Remedies include RSA 358-A:10 civil remedies with attorney's fees; unlawful lockout where the landlord re-lets the unit: damages not less than $3,000 (540-A:4, IX(a),(e)).
month_to_month_tenant_notice: No statute found setting a notice period for a tenant to end a month-to-month tenancy (RSA 540:2 and 540:3 govern notice by the lessor/owner).
month_to_month_landlord_notice: For all residential tenancies the landlord's eviction notice is 30 days (RSA 540:3, II); 7 days suffice for nonpayment of rent, substantial damage, behaviour adversely affecting health/safety, or an accused domestic-violence perpetrator (540:2, II(a),(b),(d),(h)). The notice must state the reason with specificity (540:3, III). Whether the landlord needs a stated cause depends on whether the property is 'restricted' or 'nonrestricted' (540:2, I-II; defined in RSA 540:1-a). For restricted property the permitted reasons are listed in 540:2, II(a)-(i). New 540:2, II(i), effective July 1, 2026: for a lease with an original term (or renewed total) of 12 months or longer, the landlord may end the tenancy at expiration if it gave written notice at least 60 days before the termination date that the lease will not be renewed and filed a possessory action within 6 months after the lease expired; this no-fault ending is not treated as an eviction for screening purposes (540:2, VIII). Where good cause is based on tenant conduct, a prior written warning notice is required (540:2, III).
rent_increase_notice: A tenant's refusal to agree to a rent increase is 'good cause' for eviction (restricted property) only if the landlord gave written notice of the amount and effective date of the increase at least 30 days before it takes effect (RSA 540:2, IV). No separate general statute requiring notice of a rent increase was found.
